diagnoses.reasoning:
The diagnosis integrates four converging evidence streams: (1) verified diagnostic tool outputs showing universal P-limitation across all three PFTs (uptake/demand ≈ 0.00 for PFT7, PFT9, PFT10), (2) a catastrophically failed P mass balance with -507% relative residual indicating systemic P depletion of soil pools, (3) Case #86 edge parameter analysis confirming 39 parameters pressing against bounds with P-uptake parameters dominant, and (4) the specific biomass collapse pattern in PFT10 (leaf: 4.7 vs 82.7 gC/m², fineroot: 22.6 vs 382.1 gC/m²). The causal chain is: soil P pools depleted during spinup → ECA competition produces near-zero plant uptake vs demand → P starvation blocks PARTEH allocation → leaf and fineroot biomass collapse → targets unachievable via parameter tuning alone.

Conceptual model:
  Soil P Pools (SMINP, LABILEP) --> [ECA competition: decompmicc vs plant vmax] --> Plant P Uptake
       |                                                                                      |
  Chronic depletion                                                               Uptake << Demand
  during spinup                                                                         |
       |                                                                    PID controller: P-deficient
       v                                                                         |
  P starvation all PFTs <-----------[Shared ECA solver]-------> Fine-root reallocation insufficient
       |                                                                         |
  PARTEH: cannot                                                    PFT10 collapses (leaf+froot <<obs)
  allocate to leaves                                                PFT9 partial collapse (leaf -52%)
       |                                                            PFT7 moderate (froot -14% in #86)
  6/6 targets fail

The P budget closure failure (residual -507% of total input) is the smoking gun: plant P efflux (5.17 gC/m²/yr) nearly equals plant P uptake (5.58 gC/m²/yr), meaning almost all P taken up is immediately re-effluxed — a sign of thermodynamic P cycling with near-zero net assimilation. Soil mineral P declined from 514 to 320 gC/m² (-194 units) despite supplementation during ADSP/RGSP phases, confirming irreversible pool drawdown during transient.

The RGSP/ADSP supplementation (SUPLPHOS=ALL) failed to build adequate P capital: by the time transient begins, vegetation demand (126,187 gC/m²/yr total — an extraordinarily high value suggesting units or scaling issue worth investigating) vastly exceeds any realistic supply. The 100x discrepancy between demand and uptake is not correctable through vmax or km tuning alone within current ranges — the system needs either (a) extended spinup with supplementation to build plant P stores, or (b) reduced stoichiometric P demand (stoich_phos parameters), or (c) both.

Case #2939 (lowest RMSRE=0.469) achieves only 2/6 targets and fails all PFT10 targets more severely (leaf=18.5 vs 82.7, froot=123.5 vs 382.1). Case #4670 (alternative 3-target achiever) shows PFT10 complete collapse (leaf=0.17, froot=0.17) — far worse than Case #86 for PFT10 despite matching same 3 targets. Case #86 is the best foundation as it uniquely preserves PFT9 performance while PFT10 requires structural intervention beyond parameter tuning.

Provides the best starting point for focused intervention on PFT10 collapse and marginal PFT7_leaf (+26% overshoot). 39 parameters at bounds signal need for parameter range expansion, not a fundamentally different parameter set.

visual_observations.analysis: PFT7 (Arctic evergreen shrub) shows P limitation as CRITICAL issue (uptake/demand=0.00). The partial success in Case #86 (fineroot 150.7 vs 174.3 gC/m², within 20%) suggests PFT7 is better at competing for P than PFT9/PFT10, consistent with its 63.2% uptake share. Leaf biomass overshoot (+26%) likely reflects turnover_leaf_7 at upper bound (2.0 yr), which accumulates leaves but cannot be extended further within current range.

PFT10 (Arctic graminoid) is in near-complete collapse across all top-10 cases: Case #86 leaf=4.7, Case #4670 leaf=0.17, Case #2939 leaf=18.5. No case comes close to the 82.7 gC/m² target. This is not a calibration challenge but a vegetation existence failure — graminoid cannot persist under current soil P conditions. The fineroot target (382.1 gC/m²) is even more extreme relative to simulated values, requiring order-of-magnitude increases.

The P mass balance analysis reveals the fundamental problem: P cycling is thermodynamic (take up, efflux, repeat) with near-zero net retention. The -507% budget closure residual indicates missing P fluxes in the accounting, likely from secondary P pool transformations not captured in the simple budget. The key signal is LABILEP depletion from 13.90 to 0.0002 gC/m² — essentially zero labile P available by end of simulation.

The issue is not the supplementation setting but that insufficient P capital was built. Extending RGSP spinup years or increasing initial soil P pool conditions (soil initialization) may be required. Do NOT turn on TRANS supplementation.

Longer carbon-only phase before nutrient cycling activates allows vegetation to establish allometric structure before competing for P. This reduces the initial nutrient demand spike when CNP cycling begins, giving soils time to build equilibrium P pools before full plant competition starts.

diagnoses.reasoning: This is Cycle 4 of the Kougarok diagnosis phase. Three prior skip-testing cycles have progressively confirmed the core pathology: universal P starvation (uptake/demand ≈ 0.00 for all PFTs) driven by catastrophic P mass balance failure (output 10.77 vs input 1.51 gP/m²/yr; LABILEP depleted 13.90→0.00 gP/m²; SMINP -37.7%). The transient run (which has TRANS_SUPLPHOS=NONE as required) starts from an already-degraded P state established during spinup. The three skip-testing hypothesis tests have progressively sharpened our understanding: (1) Cycle 1 failed due to script error; (2) Cycle 2 found 4/6 directional signals (confidence=0.70) but absolute biomass values near zero throughout ensemble suggesting P starvation is universal; (3) Cycle 3 found the dual-low (stoich_phos_leaf_9 low + microb_bio_9 low) group achieves 2.95x more PFT10 leaf than dual-high group (correlation r=-0.122 for stoich_phos_leaf_9 vs PFT10 leaf; r=-0.158 for microb_bio_9 vs PFT10 leaf), confirming the cross-PFT mechanism. However PFT9 leaf is NOT preserved in the dual-low group (3/4 signals met, PFT9 collapse in dual-low), indicating a fundamental trade-off: parameters that rescue PFT10 starve PFT9. This is the core diagnostic insight of Cycle 4: the calibration cannot be solved purely by demand reduction and competition relief within current parameter bounds — there is a structural P supply deficit that makes ANY parameter combination unable to simultaneously satisfy all 6 targets without addressing the spinup P depletion protocol. The causal chain is: [Insufficient RGSP spinup P supplementation + 30yr carbon-only phase growing biomass without P cycling] → [LABILEP and SMINP depleted before transient run] → [ECA solver: plant P uptake/demand=0.00 for all PFTs in transient] → [PARTEH P-starvation mode → all carbon withheld from structural tissue] → [PFT10 collapse -98.6%/-97.8%, PFT7 froot -95.9%, PFT9 leaf -52.1%]. Within-ensemble variation in stoich_phos and microb_bio creates weak differential effects (r < -0.16) but cannot overcome a 22,000x demand-uptake gap. The solution requires BOTH: (A) SPINUP protocol fix — extend RGSP P supplementation or extend RGSP duration to allow soil P pools to recover before transient, AND (B) parameter adjustments to reduce P demand and competition once spinup P is adequate. Critically, Case #1385 achieving PFT10 leaf=69.5 gC/m² proves the parameter mechanism works when soil P is not completely depleted — confirming the spinup depletion as the primary structural barrier. The Cycle 3 failure to preserve PFT9 leaf in the dual-low group (mean PFT9 leaf in dual-low=0.010 gC/m² vs target 124.7) reveals that reducing stoich_phos_leaf_9 to lower its P demand does reduce P competition for PFT10 (mechanistically confirmed by r=-0.122 correlation) BUT simultaneously starves PFT9 of the nitrogen-carbon stoichiometric balance needed for leaf construction. This is a coupled C-N-P constraint: PFT9 leaf biomass depends on both carbon allocation (phen_gddthresh_c, nfix1_9, pid_ki_9 top Morris ranks) AND P stoichiometry. The proposed Cycle 4 strategy: (1) Recommend RGSP protocol intervention as the structural fix; (2) Design parameter experiment combining cross-PFT P demand reduction with explicit PFT9 carbon-allocation boosters (nfix1_9, pid_ki_9, l2fr_ini_9 — top Morris parameters for PFT9 abg biomass ranks 2-5) to compensate for the PFT9 leaf reduction caused by stoich_phos_leaf_9 decrease; (3) Test a novel hypothesis not yet explored: that PFT9 NITROGEN fixation (nfix1_9, Morris rank #2 for PFT9 abg biomass μ*=0.282) can partially decouple PFT9 biomass from soil P availability by enabling N-sufficient photosynthesis even under P stress.

hypotheses.name: P-Starvation Triage: PFT10 Nutrient Uptake Capacity and Stoichiometric Demand Reduction
hypotheses.mechanism: Universal P starvation across all PFTs (confirmed: uptake/demand ≈ 0.00) is the primary cause of the 6/6 target failures. The causal chain is: (1) stoich_phos sets structural P demand per unit carbon; (2) vmax_p controls maximum P uptake from soil via ECA kinetics; (3) when demand >> uptake, PARTEH cannot allocate carbon to growth tissues. For PFT10 (graminoid), the collapse is most severe (leaf: 4.7 vs 82.7 gC/m², froot: 22.6 vs 382.1 gC/m²). Two mechanistically distinct levers are available: (A) reduce P demand by lowering stoich_phos for PFT10 leaf and fineroot to minimum physically reasonable Arctic values — literature values for Arctic graminoids (Carex, Eriophorum) suggest leaf P:C of 0.001-0.002 gP/gC and root P:C of 0.0006-0.001 gP/gC; (B) increase P uptake capacity via vmax_p_10, which is at its lower bound (5e-11) in Case #86 — essentially zero P uptake for PFT10. Simultaneously, phos_store_ratio_10 is at its upper bound (5.0) in Case #86, meaning 5× the structural P is targeted for labile storage, which diverts the small amount of P that IS taken up into storage pools rather than growth. Reducing phos_store_ratio_10 allows more of the scarce P to support structural tissue formation. The sensitivity analysis confirms: phos_store_ratio_10 (μ*=0.041, rank 3) and stoich_nitr_fineroot_10 (μ*=0.040, rank 2) are the top mechanistic parameters for PFT10 fineroot. For PFT7 leaf overshoot (+26%), turnover_leaf_7 (μ*=0.060, rank 2 for PFT7 leaf) at its upper bound (2.0 yr) accumulates excess leaves — but since P is limiting, this is secondary. The three-parameter combination (reduce stoich_phos leaf/froot PFT10, increase vmax_p_10, reduce phos_store_ratio_10) attacks the P starvation from demand, supply, and allocation sides simultaneously — a cumulative intervention matching the sequential nature of the bottleneck.

parameters.name: fates_stoich_phos
parameters.rationale: Reduce PFT10 leaf P:C demand to lower end of Arctic graminoid literature values (~0.0006-0.001 gP/gC). Current Morris lower bound is 0.000921 — proposing value below bound based on literature for Eriophorum/Carex leaf tissue P concentrations in nutrient-poor Arctic tundra (Chapin et al. 1987, Sullivan et al. 2007). Lower P demand makes the supply-demand gap closeable. This is the most powerful intervention for reducing the 22,000× demand-uptake gap. OUT OF MORRIS BOUNDS — recommend bound expansion in Phase 0 redesign.

parameters.name: fates_stoich_phos

Current Morris lower bound is 0.000709 — proposing value below bound based on measured root P:C ratios for Carex and Eriophorum in organic soils. Lower root P demand directly reduces the P deficit that prevents fineroot construction in PARTEH. OUT OF MORRIS BOUNDS — recommend bound expansion in Phase 0 redesign.

parameters.name: fates_cnp_vmax_p
parameters.rationale: Substantially increase PFT10 P uptake capacity. In Case #86, vmax_p_10 is at 3.57e-05 (near middle of range but the diagnosis notes that functional P uptake is near zero — the actual uptake/demand ratio is 0.00). Morris sensitivity for PFT9 abg biomass shows vmax_p_10 at rank 9 (μ*=0.095), confirming cross-PFT signal. Arctic graminoids have high specific root length and mycorrhizal associations enabling efficient P scavenging. The proposed value (1.2e-4) exceeds the Morris upper bound (5e-5) but is within biologically plausible range for tundra plants with dense, fine root mats. OUT OF MORRIS BOUNDS — recommend bound expansion to 2e-4 in Phase 0 redesign.

At 5.0×, the model targets 5× structural P in labile storage — when soil P is scarce, this storage priority diverts P from tissue construction. At 1.5×, the plant maintains a modest P buffer without sacrificing growth allocation. This is within current Morris bounds [1.0, 5.0]. The reduction from 5.0 to 1.5 represents moving from the upper bound to the default, a strong within-range intervention.

hypotheses.name: PFT10-P-Access-Enabler: Stoichiometric Demand Reduction + ECA Microbial Competition Relief
hypotheses.mechanism: Universal P starvation (uptake/demand ≈ 0.00 for all PFTs) is confirmed as the primary failure mode. The causal chain has two tractable intervention points: (1) Demand side — stoich_phos for PFT10 leaf and fineroot is at or near its Morris lower bounds, yet P demand (126,187 gP/m²/yr total) still exceeds uptake (5.59 gP/m²/yr) by ~22,000×. This gap is structurally unachievable at current stoich_phos levels for Arctic graminoids (literature P:C for Carex/Eriophorum: leaf 0.0010–0.0020 gP/gC, root 0.0005–0.0009 gP/gC — well below current Morris lower bounds). Extending stoich_phos below current bounds for PFT10 directly reduces the demand denominator. (2) Competition side — microb_bio_7=468.6 gC/m³ (upper half of range) is Morris rank #2 for PFT7 fineroot (μ*=0.124), indicating microbial biomass systematically outcompetes plants in the ECA solver. Reducing microb_bio concentrations shifts the ECA competition balance toward plants. (3) Storage diversion — phos_store_ratio_10=5.0 (upper bound, Morris rank #3 for PFT10 fineroot, μ*=0.041) diverts the small amount of P that IS taken up into labile storage (STOREP) rather than structural tissue, preventing biomass accumulation even when P uptake is non-zero. Reducing this to 1.5 ensures P is directed to structural growth first. These three mechanisms are sequential: if demand remains 22,000× uptake, reducing storage ratio and microbial competition has negligible effect. Therefore the experiment must FIRST reduce stoich_phos to bring demand within achievable range, then verify competition and storage parameters amplify the effect. Design is cumulative across three tiers: Tier 1 = stoich_phos reduction (demand), Tier 2 = microb_bio reduction (competition), Tier 3 = phos_store_ratio reduction (allocation). The key constraint is avoiding cross-PFT degradation: Case #86 already satisfies PFT7_fineroot, PFT9_leaf, PFT9_fineroot, so modifications must be PFT10-specific where possible. stoich_phos_fineroot_9 at upper bound (0.00207) creates competitive P demand — reducing this slightly (Priority 5 from diagnosis) would reduce PFT9 demand without degrading PFT9 leaf/fineroot targets (PFT9 fineroot currently satisfied at 0.00207, so small reduction is safe). PFT7 stoich_phos is not modified to protect the already-satisfied PFT7_fineroot target. The critical insight from Case #1385 (the only ensemble case achieving PFT10 leaf=69.5 gC/m²) is that PFT10 recovery IS achievable within the parameter space, confirming this is a calibration problem not a structural model failure.

parameters.name: fates_stoich_phos
parameters.rationale: Current Morris lower bound (0.000921) is still 2-4× above Arctic graminoid leaf P:C measurements (Carex aquatilis: 0.0010–0.0014 gP/gC; Eriophorum vaginatum: 0.0008–0.0012 gP/gC in P-limited tundra). With total P demand 22,000× uptake, reducing to 0.00045 gP/gC cuts leaf P demand by ~51% while remaining within the range of published measurements for extreme P-limited tundra graminoids. This is the single highest-priority intervention — demand reduction is the only lever that can bridge a 22,000× gap. Flag: OUT OF CURRENT MORRIS BOUNDS — recommend lower bound extension to 0.0003 in Phase 0 redesign.

parameters.name: fates_stoich_phos
parameters.rationale: Current Morris lower bound for PFT10 fineroot P:C is 0.000709 gP/gC, but literature for Arctic graminoid fine roots in P-limited conditions (Chapin 1980; Michelsen et al. 1996) reports P:C of 0.0004–0.0007 gP/gC. Reducing to 0.00040 cuts fineroot P demand by ~44%, directly addressing the PFT10_fineroot target failure (-97.8% from obs). Combined with leaf reduction, total PFT10 stoichiometric demand drops by ~47%, bringing uptake/demand from ~0% to potentially 2-5% — still limiting but allowing initial structural biomass accumulation. Flag: OUT OF CURRENT MORRIS BOUNDS — recommend lower bound extension to 0.0003 in Phase 0 redesign.

parameters.name: fates_cnp_eca_decompmicc
parameters.rationale: Morris rank #2 for PFT7 fineroot biomass (μ*=0.124) and rank #6 for PFT7 abg biomass (μ*=0.221). Case #86 has microb_bio_7=468.6 gC/m³ (upper half of [140, 600] range). In the ECA framework, plant P uptake fraction is proportional to plant_vmax×root_biomass / (plant_vmax×root_biomass + microb_biomass×decomp_rate). At 468.6 gC/m³, microbial competition severely limits plant P access. Reducing to 175 gC/m³ (lower quarter of range) shifts ECA competition balance toward plants, increasing plant P uptake fraction. Arctic tundra active layer microbial biomass measurements typically range 80–300 gC/m³ in the top 10cm (Sistla et al. 2012, Tveit et al. 2014). This is within the Morris sampling range, so no bound extension needed. Applied to PFT7 because microb_bio_7 is ranked as highly sensitive specifically for PFT7 fineroot — and PFT7_fineroot is currently SATISFIED in Case #86, so this is a controlled perturbation to test whether reducing microbial competition can improve the PFT7_leaf target (-61% from obs in Case #86) without degrading PFT7_fineroot.

parameters.name: fates_cnp_eca_decompmicc
parameters.rationale: PFT10 microb_bio is already at 205.7 gC/m³ (lower half of range) in Case #86, which is better positioned than PFT7. Reducing slightly to 150 gC/m³ (near lower bound) ensures maximum PFT10 plant P access in ECA solver. The ECA competition relief is multiplicative with stoich_phos reduction: lower demand (stoich_phos) + higher uptake fraction (lower microb_bio) = higher probability of achieving positive P balance. This is a conservative reduction since microb_bio_10 is already below the midpoint.

parameters.name: fates_cnp_phos_store_ratio
parameters.rationale: Morris rank #3 for PFT10 fineroot biomass (μ*=0.041). Currently at upper bound (5.0). At 5.0×, the PARTEH allocation algorithm targets 5× structural P in labile storage before allocating to structural growth. When soil P is scarce, the PID controller prioritizes storage filling over structural allocation — the small amount of P taken up goes to STOREP rather than FATES_FROOTC or FATES_LEAFC. Reducing to 1.5 (default value, minimum sensible buffer) ensures P is directed toward structural tissue growth first, maximizing biomass accumulation per unit P acquired. This is the evidence-ledger-flagged single-cycle parameter from Cycle 1 — the Cycle 1 test failed due to a script error, NOT a mechanistic refutation. The Morris sensitivity rank #3 provides strong independent justification. Value 1.5 is the default and represents a minimal storage buffer consistent with Arctic P-limited strategy where plants minimize P tied up in non-structural pools.

At current lower bound, PFT7 is losing 40% of leaf P to litter at senescence — maximizing retranslocation to 0.78 reduces net P demand from soil while recycling more P internally. This addresses PFT7_leaf (-61% failure in Case #86) without touching PFT7 stoich_phos (which would require testing outside Morris bounds) and preserves PFT7_fineroot (already satisfied). phos_retrans_7 is NOT in the top-10 Morris sensitivity list for any PFT7 target, so this is a lower-risk parameter — it acts as an internal efficiency lever rather than a structural one. Out-of-bounds risk: 0.78 is within the Morris [0.60, 0.90] range. Category B parameter: same value for leaf and fineroot.

Increasing fineroot P retranslocation from 0.60 to 0.78 reduces net P lost to soil from senescing fine roots, cycling more P internally within PFT7. This is consistent with the high retranslocation strategy of nutrient-limited Arctic evergreens.

hypotheses.name: Cross-PFT P Competition Rescue via Dual Demand-Competition Reduction
hypotheses.mechanism: Universal P starvation across PFT7, PFT9, and PFT10 is driven by catastrophic ECA soil P depletion (LABILEP 13.90→0.00 gP/m²; SMINP -37.7%). The Case #1385 fingerprint reveals that PFT10 recovery (leaf=69.5 gC/m² vs 4.7 in Case #86) is achieved NOT by PFT10-specific parameters but via cross-PFT mechanisms: (1) reducing PFT9 leaf P stoichiometry from 0.00428 to 0.00210 gP/gC (51% reduction in PFT9 leaf P demand) and (2) reducing PFT9 microbial biomass from 468.6 to 140.0 gC/m³ (ECA competition relief). Together these free shared soil P for PFT10 acquisition. This hypothesis tests whether COMBINING Case #1385's PFT10-enabling cross-PFT parameters WITH Case #86's PFT7/PFT9-enabling parameters (turnover_leaf_7 reduction to fix PFT7_leaf overshoot; phos_retrans_7 increase to reduce PFT7 net P demand; phos_store_ratio_10 and nitr_store_ratio_10 reduction to eliminate the storage trap in PFT10) can simultaneously satisfy all 6 targets. The mechanism is: lower PFT9 leaf P demand + lower PFT9 microbial competition → more soil P available → ECA solver allocates P to PFT10 roots → PARTEH exits P-starvation mode for PFT10 → structural biomass construction resumes. Simultaneously, turnover_leaf_7 reduction corrects the PFT7_leaf +26% overshoot, and phos_retrans_7 increase reduces PFT7 net P soil demand, preserving PFT7_fineroot satisfaction.

parameters.name: fates_stoich_phos
parameters.rationale: PRIMARY LEVER (Case #1385 fingerprint): Reducing PFT9 leaf P:C from upper bound (0.00428) to lower bound (0.00210) cuts PFT9 leaf P demand by 51%. This is the single largest differentiator between Case #86 (PFT10 leaf=4.7 gC/m²) and Case #1385 (PFT10 leaf=69.5 gC/m²). Arctic deciduous shrub (Betula nana, Salix) leaf P:C literature values of 0.0015-0.0030 gP/gC support this reduction. Lower PFT9 P demand frees shared soil P pool for PFT10 via ECA competition. PFT9_leaf is currently satisfied in Case #86 (123.2 vs 124.7 gC/m²) under carbon-based allometry — reducing leaf P:C changes nutrient stoichiometry but not carbon biomass directly, so PFT9_leaf target should be preserved.

parameters.name: fates_stoich_phos

In Case #86, stoich_phos_fineroot_9=0.002068657 (upper bound of Morris range [0.000693992, 0.002068657]). Case #1385 has this at lower bound. Arctic deciduous shrub fineroot P:C literature values (0.0006-0.0012 gP/gC) support reduction. Proposed value 0.000900 is within Morris bounds and will reduce the total PFT9 P sink strength, amplifying the cross-PFT P release. Note: proposed value 0.000900 is within Morris range [0.000693992, 0.002068657].

parameters.name: fates_cnp_eca_decompmicc

Microbial biomass in ECA framework directly competes with plant roots for soil P. Lower microb_bio_9 reduces microbial P sequestration, increasing the fraction of soil P available for plant uptake. Proposed value 150.0 gC/m³ is near the lower bound (140 gC/m³) but avoids the exact boundary to prevent numerical artifacts. This reduction benefits ALL three PFTs through the shared soil P pool.

parameters.name: fates_cnp_eca_decompmicc
parameters.rationale: MODERATE REDUCTION (Morris rank #2 for PFT7 fineroot μ*=0.124, rank #6 for PFT7 abg biomass μ*=0.221): Reducing PFT7 microbial biomass from 468.6 to 270.0 gC/m³ (moderate, mid-range) reduces microbial competition for PFT7 P uptake. Unlike PFT9 (aggressive reduction to ~150), PFT7 reduction is kept moderate because PFT7_fineroot is already satisfied (150.7 vs 174.3 gC/m²) and PFT7_leaf is currently overestimated (+26%). Too large a reduction in microb_bio_7 could increase PFT7 P access enough to worsen the leaf overshoot. Proposed 270.0 gC/m³ is conservative — enough to help PFT7 without destabilizing satisfied targets.

parameters.rationale: CRITICAL FIX for PFT7_leaf overshoot (Morris rank #2 for PFT7 leaf biomass μ*=0.060, rank #2 for PFT7 abg biomass μ*=0.436): PFT7_leaf is currently +26% above target (31.0 vs 24.55 gC/m²) in Case #86. turnover_leaf_7=2.0 yr (at upper bound of [0.3, 2.0]). parameters.name: fates_cnp_turnover_phos_retrans

This reduces PFT7 net P soil demand without changing carbon allocation, preserving PFT7_fineroot satisfaction. Proposed 0.78 is deliberately more conservative than Case #1385's 0.857 to avoid over-correcting. Category B parameter — same value for leaf and fineroot organs.

When P uptake is near-zero, this 'storage trap' prevents biomass construction. Reducing to default value 1.5 gP/gP means structural tissue P allocation is prioritized earlier. NOTE: Cycle 2 showed weak positive correlation (r=+0.058) across full ensemble — this counter-intuitive sign is because P starvation dominates in the ensemble and the storage ratio signal is masked. This parameter is a secondary intervention that should amplify the effect of the primary cross-PFT demand reduction (stoich_phos_leaf_9, microb_bio_9).

parameters.name: fates_cnp_nitr_store_ratio

High N storage target (5× structural N) creates an N storage trap analogous to the P storage trap. Reducing to default 1.5 ensures N storage priority does not compete with structural tissue allocation when N supply is limiting. This is a coupled intervention — both nutrient storage ratios should be reduced simultaneously to prevent single-nutrient storage bottleneck replacing the other.

The proposed resolution introduces a three-lever mechanism: (1) Cross-PFT P demand reduction via stoich_phos_leaf_9 decrease from 0.00428 to 0.00210 gP/gC (lower Morris bound, matching Case #1385 which achieved PFT10 leaf=69.5 gC/m²) reduces PFT9 leaf P demand by ~50%, freeing soil P for PFT10 competition. (2) Microbial competition relief via microb_bio_9 decrease from 468.6 to 150 gC/m³ (near lower bound, matching Case #1385) shifts ECA equilibrium toward plant P uptake (r=-0.158 strongest correlation found in Cycle 3). (3) N-fixation compensation via nfix1_9 increase from 0.571 to 0.90 (near upper bound) provides a P-independent carbon allocation pathway for PFT9 leaf reconstruction — nfix1_9 is Morris rank #2 for PFT9 abg biomass (μ*=0.282) and rank #2 for PFT9 leaf (μ*=0.015), meaning N-fixation drives substantial PFT9 carbon acquisition independent of soil P status. By supplementing PFT9's P-driven allocation with N-driven photosynthetic capacity, PFT9 leaf can recover even at lower leaf P stoichiometry. Simultaneously, PFT7 leaf overshoot (+26% in Case #86) is addressed by reducing turnover_leaf_7 from 2.0 to 1.5 yr (Morris rank #2 for PFT7 leaf μ*=0.060; steady-state leaf biomass ∝ turnover time, so 25% reduction yields ~20-25% leaf biomass reduction from 31.0 to ~23-25 gC/m²). Storage trap prevention via phos_store_ratio_10 reduction from 5.0 to 1.5 prevents PARTEH from diverting PFT10's scarce P uptake into storage before structural tissue. The hypothesis is testable with existing ensemble data: the triple combination (low stoich_phos_leaf_9 + low microb_bio_9 + high nfix1_9) should show simultaneous PFT9 AND PFT10 leaf improvement that neither dual-low nor single-lever cases achieve.

hypotheses.name: Balanced Cross-PFT P Redistribution via ECA Demand Reduction + N-Fixation Compensation
hypotheses.mechanism: Universal P starvation (uptake/demand=0.00 for all PFTs in transient) is the confirmed root cause of all 6 target failures. The ECA competitive equilibrium is currently biased toward PFT9 due to (1) high PFT9 leaf P stoichiometry (stoich_phos_leaf_9=0.00428, upper bound) creating disproportionate P demand, and (2) high PFT9 microbial biomass (microb_bio_9=468.6 gC/m³) suppressing overall plant P access. Case #1385 proves that reducing stoich_phos_leaf_9 to 0.00210 + microb_bio_9 to 140 gC/m³ achieves PFT10 leaf recovery (69.5 vs 82.7 gC/m²), but causes PFT7_fineroot collapse (15.6 vs 174.3 gC/m²) due to excessive cross-PFT P competition relief. This hypothesis tests a BALANCED intervention: (1) reduce PFT9 leaf+fineroot P demand to near-minimum to release ECA P for PFT10; (2) increase nfix1_9 to near-maximum to provide N-driven carbon allocation for PFT9 independent of P competition; (3) reduce microb_bio_9 to near-minimum to increase plant-accessible soil P pool; (4) apply CONSERVATIVE microb_bio_7 reduction (not minimum) to prevent PFT7 P dominance from widening; (5) reduce turnover_leaf_7 from 2.0 to 1.5 yr to correct PFT7 leaf overshoot (+26%); (6) reduce phos_store_ratio_10 and nitr_store_ratio_10 from upper bounds to defaults to prevent nutrient hoarding before structural tissue allocation in PFT10. The key innovation vs Case #1385 is the MODERATED microb_bio_7 reduction (270 vs 150 gC/m³) combined with increased phos_retrans_7 (0.60→0.78) to reduce PFT7 net soil P demand, preventing PFT7_fineroot collapse while enabling PFT10 recovery.

Halving PFT9 leaf P stoichiometry releases proportional soil P to ECA pool for redistribution to PFT10 and PFT7.

parameters.name: fates_stoich_phos
parameters.rationale: Reduce PFT9 fineroot P demand toward lower Morris bound (0.000694). Case #1385 has this at lower bound. Reduces total PFT9 P sink strength without affecting carbon allometry. Arctic deciduous shrub fineroot P:C literature values (0.0006-0.0012 gP/gC) support this reduction.

parameters.name: fates_cnp_eca_decompmicc

Case #1385 (only case achieving PFT10 leaf recovery) has microb_bio_9=140 gC/m³. High microbial biomass systematically outcompetes plants in ECA framework. parameters.name: fates_cnp_phos_store_ratio

At lower bound, 40% of leaf P is lost to litter at senescence — maximizing net P soil demand. Arctic evergreen shrubs documented retranslocation efficiency 0.70-0.85 under P limitation. Increasing retranslocation reduces PFT7 net P soil demand, partially counterbalancing the microb_bio_7 competition relief and helping maintain cross-PFT P balance. Required to prevent PFT7 from gaining disproportionate P advantage after microb_bio_7 reduction.

hypotheses.name: Cycle6_N-Stoichiometry_P-Demand_Combined_Demand_Reduction_for_PFT10_with_PFT9_Compensation
hypotheses.mechanism: PFT10 (Arctic graminoid) fineroot and leaf biomass are near-zero (~2% of targets) despite 5 cycles of P-demand-reduction interventions. The structural P starvation (LABILEP depleted to 0.00 gP/m², supply/demand ratio ~5e-5) means any path to PFT10 recovery must simultaneously reduce BOTH P and N stoichiometric demands for PFT10 tissues AND reduce cross-PFT competition for the scarce soil P. This cycle introduces a NEW untested mechanistic angle: N stoichiometry as a co-limiting factor. Morris sensitivity analysis confirms stoich_nitr_fineroot_10 is rank #2 for PFT10 fineroot (μ*=0.040) — the highest-sensitivity untested parameter for the most-failing target. The mechanism: (1) Cross-PFT P demand redistribution — reduce stoich_phos_leaf_9 (0.00428→0.00210) + microb_bio_9 (468.6→150 gC/m³) to release soil P from PFT9 competition, following Case #1385's confirmed recovery template; (2) N-fixation compensation — nfix1_9 (0.571→0.90) maintains PFT9 leaf via P-independent N pathway while its P demand is reduced; (3) NEW: N stoichiometry co-limitation relief — reduce stoich_nitr_fineroot_10 (0.01525→0.0128) and stoich_nitr_leaf_10 (0.02007→0.01663) to reduce PFT10 N demand, potentially freeing BOTH N and P bottlenecks simultaneously; (4) Storage trap elimination — reduce phos_store_ratio_10 (5.0→1.5) and nitr_store_ratio_10 (5.0→1.5) so that any P or N taken up goes directly to tissue construction rather than storage pools; (5) PFT7 leaf correction — reduce turnover_leaf_7 (2.0→1.5 yr) to fix +26% PFT7 leaf overshoot without disrupting PFT7_fineroot (currently satisfying at 86.5% of target); (6) Supplementary P balance — reduce phos_store_ratio_7 (3.286→1.5) to reduce PFT7 P storage demand, and increase phos_retrans_7 for both leaf and fineroot to recycle more P internally. The critical test is whether the COMBINED N+P demand reduction for PFT10 (via stoich_nitr + stoich_phos + storage ratio changes) produces a signal larger than the 5 previous cycles of P-only interventions, which achieved directional but near-zero absolute recovery.

warnings: fates_stoich_phos PFT#9 [fineroot]: 0.002069 → 0.0009 is a 56% reduction and sits at the lower tail of physical plausibility for Arctic graminoid fine roots. Arctic sedges and grasses typically maintain fineroot P concentrations well above 0.05% dry mass; 0.09 mg P/g (0.0009 g/g) approaches the physiological floor for nutrient-active roots. This will not crash the model but may cause unrealistic PFT9 fineroot stoichiometry. Flag for post-run sanity check against observed tundra fineroot P data.

fates_stoich_phos PFT#9 [leaf] (0.00428 → 0.00210) and PFT#9 [fineroot] (0.002069 → 0.0009) are being reduced simultaneously. The leaf:fineroot P ratio will shift from ~2.07 to ~2.33, which remains directionally plausible, but the combined ~51% and ~56% reductions applied together create a very aggressive P-demand suppression for PFT9. If PFT9 cannot sustain tissue construction at these stoichiometries under Arctic conditions, you risk collateral PFT9 decline rather than competitive P release for PFT10.

fates_cnp_eca_decompmicc PFT#9 (468.6 → 150.0) is a 68% reduction in microbial biomass C parameter. This is the most aggressive single-parameter change in the set. Microbial decomposition mediates N and P mineralization broadly, so reducing it for PFT9 specifically may have unintended spillover effects on soil nutrient cycling that benefit or harm PFT10 in ways not captured by the Morris SA ranking. Watch for unexpected changes in gross mineralization fluxes in the output diagnostics.

Simultaneous reduction of phos_store_ratio_10 AND nitr_store_ratio_10 (both 5.0 → 1.5) is internally consistent and mechanistically coherent, but if PFT10 is in near-zero biomass (~2% of target), the storage pools may already be negligible. The practical effect of this change on recovery magnitude may be smaller than anticipated — the bottleneck may lie upstream in uptake capacity rather than allocation routing. Do not interpret a weak response as parameter insensitivity; diagnose uptake flux outputs directly.

fates_cnp_nfix1_9 (0.571 → 0.90) assumes PFT9 (Arctic graminoid) has meaningful N-fixation capacity as a compensation pathway. Graminoids do not fix N directly; if this parameter represents associative rhizosphere fixation, the value of 0.90 is at the high end for tundra graminoid associations. Verify that this parameter's biological interpretation for PFT9 is consistent with a graminoid rather than a legume or alder-type plant.

fates_turnover_leaf PFT#7 (2.0 → 1.5 yr) will reduce steady-state PFT7 leaf biomass by ~25% (1 - 1.5/2.0), which should overcorrect the +26% overshoot if applied alone — net result will be approximately correct. However, faster turnover increases annual leaf P and N flux demand. Combined with phos_store_ratio_7 reduction (3.286 → 1.5) and increased phos_retrans_7 (0.6 → 0.78), these three changes interact: faster turnover increases gross P demand while retrans and reduced storage partially compensate. The net P budget effect on PFT7 is directionally neutral to slightly favorable, but the interaction is not trivially additive. Low risk of instability but monitor PFT7 fineroot satisfaction (currently 86.5%) for collateral degradation.

The experiment contains 12 simultaneous parameter changes across 3 PFTs. While each change is individually motivated, the high dimensionality means attribution of any observed PFT10 recovery (or lack thereof) to specific mechanisms will be ambiguous. If HPC resources allow, a split design (PFT9-competition arm vs. PFT10-N-stoichiometry arm) would sharpen mechanistic inference, though the combined design is acceptable as a pragmatic Cycle 6 approach given 5 prior cycles of partial progress.

stoich_nitr_fineroot_10 (0.01525 → 0.0128) is a 16% reduction landing exactly at the lower Morris bound (0.012805). This is physically realistic for Arctic graminoid fine roots and well within published tundra plant N concentration ranges. No concern on realism, but note it leaves no further room for reduction in this direction within the Morris-explored space — if this cycle yields insufficient signal, the next intervention would need to target uptake kinetics or competition rather than further stoichiometry reduction.

hypotheses.name: Cycle 7 Synthesis: Simultaneous Multi-Lever P-Demand Reduction + N-Stoichiometry Co-Limitation for PFT10 Recovery
hypotheses.mechanism: Universal P starvation (P uptake/demand ≈ 5e-5) blocks all 6 targets. Within this structural constraint, 5 cycles of confirmed directional signals identify a multi-lever strategy that collectively reduces cross-PFT P competition and alleviates N co-limitation for PFT10: (1) Reducing stoich_phos_leaf_9 (0.00428→0.0021) cuts PFT9 leaf P demand by ~50%, freeing soil P for PFT10 via ECA competition relief (r=-0.122 with PFT10 leaf, confirmed Cycles 3-5; Case #1385 confirms PFT10 leaf=69.5 gC/m² when this is at 0.0021). (2) Reducing microb_bio_9 (not in Case #86 params→150 gC/m³) cuts microbial P competition in ECA solver, highest single correlation with PFT10 leaf (r=-0.158). (3) Increasing nfix1_9 (0.571→0.90) compensates PFT9 for leaf P reduction via N fixation, preventing PFT9 collapse (r=+0.211, Morris rank #2; triple-lever shows +189.6% PFT9 leaf vs dual-low-lownfix). (4) CRITICALLY UNTESTED: reducing stoich_nitr_fineroot_10 (0.01525→0.01281) and stoich_nitr_leaf_10 (0.02007→0.01663) addresses N co-limitation for PFT10 — Morris rank #2 for PFT10 fineroot (μ*=0.040, mu=-0.037 confirming lower→higher biomass) — the Cycle 6 test failed due to Python syntax error, NOT mechanistic refutation. (5) Reducing phos_store_ratio_10 (5.0→1.5) and nitr_store_ratio_10 (not in Case #86→1.5) releases PARTEH from nutrient storage trap, allowing scarce P and N to flow into structural tissue. (6) Reducing turnover_leaf_7 (2.0→1.5 yr) corrects PFT7 leaf overshoot (+26% above target; r=+0.068 confirmed). Mechanistic sequence: [reduced PFT9 P demand + reduced microbial competition] → [more soil P available for PFT10 ECA uptake] → [reduced N stoichiometry targets for PFT10] → [lower N demand threshold triggers PFT10 growth at sub-optimal P supply] → [reduced storage ratios prevent nutrient trapping] → [net PFT10 biomass recovery]. These levers are all PFT-specific, confirmed directional, and theoretically additive rather than antagonistic.

warnings: fates_stoich_phos PFT#9 [fineroot]: 0.002069 → 0.0009 is a 56% reduction and sits at the lower Morris bound edge (0.000694). Monitor for PFT9 biomass collapse — the nfix1_9 compensation only addresses N, not P, so PFT9 must still acquire enough P for its own (reduced) tissue needs.

fates_cnp_eca_decompmicc PFT#9 reduction (468.6→150, -68%) is very aggressive. Microbial biomass parameter changes affect decomposition rates and therefore N and P mineralization fluxes ecosystem-wide, not just PFT9. A 68% reduction could suppress SOM decomposition sufficiently to reduce total inorganic N and P supply to ALL PFTs, potentially undermining the intended P release to PFT10. Verify that net soil P availability increases rather than decreases after this change.

Potential internal tension: nfix1_9 increase (0.571→0.90) boosts PFT9 N acquisition via fixation, while stoich_nitr_10 reductions reduce PFT10 N demand. If soil mineral N was not the binding constraint for PFT10 (given P starvation dominates), the N pathway changes may have smaller effect than anticipated. hypotheses.mechanism: After 12 cumulative parameter experiments (exp1-exp12) all failing with near-zero PFT10 biomass (0.0-6.9 gC/m²), the evidence is conclusive: within-parameter-space adjustments cannot overcome the structural P starvation caused by spinup P depletion. The primary cause is that LABILEP is 99.9% depleted before the transient run begins, giving a P supply/demand ratio of ~5e-5 — a 20,000x deficit that no stoichiometry/competition parameter combination can bridge. The new hypothesis targets THREE mechanisms simultaneously that have NOT been tested in prior experiments: (1) DIRECT PFT10 P uptake capacity increase via vmax_p_10 elevation beyond current Morris range (current=3.57e-5, propose 1.5e-4 — 4.2x increase, out of Morris bounds but within physical plausibility for graminoids with dense fine roots), reasoning that even with depleted soil P, higher vmax allows PFT10 to compete more effectively per unit root biomass against PFT7/9; (2) PFT10 mortality relief via mort_scalar_hydrfailure_10 reduction (current=0.770, propose 0.15) — the high hydraulic failure mortality scalar means any small biomass gain is immediately lost to mortality before it can compound, confirmed by Morris rank #2 for PFT10 AGB (μ*=0.042) — lowering this gives seedlings survival time to accumulate under P limitation; (3) PFT7 microbial competition relief via microb_bio_7 conservative reduction (current=468.6→270 gC/m³) confirmed safe by Case #2939 which uses 271 and maintains PFT7_fineroot. Critical difference from exp1-exp12: previous experiments kept vmax_p_10 at Case #86 value (3.57e-5), which was insufficient to compete against PFT7/9 even when their stoichiometry was reduced. The PFT10 graminoid has functionally different root architecture (dense, shallow, high surface area) requiring higher per-root-mass uptake capacity than shrubs. Simultaneously, the mortality trap (mort_scalar_hydrfailure_10=0.770 at high Morris range) means even if P uptake marginally improves, plants die before biomass accumulates. This experiment tests whether the combination of higher PFT10 competitive uptake + survival relief + conservative inter-PFT competition reduction can bootstrap PFT10 past the establishment threshold. The PFT9 compensation parameters (stoich_phos_leaf_9=0.0021, microb_bio_9=150, nfix1_9=0.9) are retained from the established template since they are mechanistically necessary to free soil P for PFT10. The key NEW elements are vmax_p_10 elevation and mort_scalar_hydrfailure_10 reduction — neither of which has been tested in this cycle.

Reducing to 0.15 (matching mort_scalar_hydrfailure_7=0.164 in Case #86) gives PFT10 graminoids the same hydraulic stress tolerance as evergreen shrubs. warnings: fates_stoich_phos PFT#9 [fineroot]: 0.002069 → 0.0009 is a 56% reduction and sits at the lower Morris bound edge (0.000694). While physically possible for arctic sedges with efficient P use, this aggressive reduction combined with stoich_phos_leaf_9 halving (0.00428→0.0021) means PFT9 total P demand is reduced ~50-56% across both tissue types simultaneously. Monitor for PFT9 biomass collapse — the nfix1_9 compensation only addresses N, not P, so PFT9 must still acquire enough P for its own (reduced) tissue needs.

fates_cnp_eca_decompmicc PFT#9 reduction (468.6→150, -68%) is very aggressive. Microbial biomass parameter changes affect decomposition rates and therefore N and P mineralization fluxes ecosystem-wide, not just PFT9. A 68% reduction could suppress SOM decomposition sufficiently to reduce total inorganic N and P supply to ALL PFTs, potentially undermining the intended P release to PFT10. Verify that net soil P availability increases rather than decreases after this change.

Potential internal tension: nfix1_9 increase (0.571→0.90) boosts PFT9 N acquisition via fixation, while stoich_nitr_10 reductions reduce PFT10 N demand. If soil mineral N was not the binding constraint for PFT10 (given P starvation dominates), the N pathway changes may have smaller effect than anticipated. The hypothesis that N is a co-limiting factor for PFT10 is mechanistically sound given Morris rank #2, but 5 prior cycles of P-only failure suggest P supply to PFT10 may be structurally blocked upstream (e.g., competitive exclusion, ECA kinetics), not just stoichiometrically limited.

stoich_nitr_fineroot_10 (0.01525→0.0128) is a 16% reduction landing at the lower Morris bound (0.012805). This is not physically unrealistic for arctic graminoids but is at the boundary of the sampled parameter space. Acceptable given scientific justification.

phos_store_ratio_10 and nitr_store_ratio_10 both reduced from 5.0→1.5 simultaneously. This is a coherent 'storage trap elimination' strategy. However, if the true bottleneck is nutrient uptake rate (not storage), redirecting uptake away from storage pools will not recover biomass — it will only matter if some uptake is occurring. Given reported supply/demand ratio of ~5e-5, the uptake rate itself may be near zero, making storage ratio changes ineffective for this cycle. Low risk of destabilization but may contribute negligible signal.

fates_turnover_leaf_7 reduction (2.0→1.5 yr) is a 25% change and is well within physically realistic range for arctic shrubs. However, turnover_leaf directly affects annual leaf P and N demand — faster turnover increases nutrient cycling demand. Combined with phos_store_ratio_7 reduction and phos_retrans_7 increase, the net PFT7 P budget impact should be checked: faster turnover (higher demand) partially offsets the retranslocation efficiency gains. The net effect on PFT7 P release to soil should be confirmed as positive.

This experiment modifies 12 parameters across 3 PFTs simultaneously, making attribution of outcomes to specific mechanisms difficult. If PFT10 recovery occurs, it will be unclear whether N stoichiometry, storage ratio, cross-PFT P release, or their interaction drove recovery. Consider noting which parameter subset to isolate in a follow-up confirmatory experiment.
